# Kokand–Dzungar War (1742–1745)

The Kokand–Dzungar War was a conflict fought between the Dzungar Khanate and the Kokand Khanate (supported by the Kazakh Khanate and Afsharid Iran) from 1742 to 1745. Sparked by Kokand's refusal to submit to Dzungar suzerainty, the war involved a series of Dzungar invasions into Central Asia. It culminated in a decisive Kokand victory, marking the beginning of the Dzungar Khanate's decline in the region.
Background
During Nader Shah's Central Asian campaigns, the political landscape shifted. The Kokand Bek, Abdul Karim Bi, allied with Nader Shah, who provided him with military support and artillery to expand his rule and wage war against the Dzungar Kalmyks. Meanwhile, diplomatic and trade relations between Kokand and the Dzungar Khanate rapidly deteriorated after Kokandians harassed Dzungar merchants and Abdul Karim Bi refused to pay tribute to Galdan Tseren.
History
In 1742, Galdan Tseren sent a 30,000-strong army led by Septen and Dagby to conquer cities including Tashkent and Kokand. The Dzungars faced fierce, unexpected resistance. At Tashkent, Kokand forces used horse rattles to spook the Dzungar cavalry, and at Kokand, they lured the Dzungars into hidden trenches. Although the Dzungars eventually captured Tashkent with reinforcements, the campaign was ultimately stalled by heavy losses, severe frost, and a smallpox epidemic.  In the spring of 1745, the Dzungars launched a renewed offensive with up to 40,000 men  Abdul Karim Bi preemptively marched on Tashkent, forcing the Dzungar governor to flee, and installed the prominent Kazakh judge Tole Bi as co-governor. Though the Dzungars soon forced Tole Bi to evacuate the city, their commander Sary Mandzhi was poisoned by him. Facing rumors of a Russian invasion in the north and the arrival of 20,000 Persian reinforcement troops in the south, the Dzungar advance faltered.  The Dzungars attempted a final siege on Kokand but fell into another trap: the defenders allowed a portion of the army inside, slaughtered them, and collapsed a bridge, killing over 2,000 Dzungar soldiers. The siege turned into a stalemate and ended abruptly when Galdan Tseren died in September 1745. His successor immediately ordered a full withdrawal of the army back to Dzungaria.
Aftermath
The successful defense against the Dzungar invasion cemented Abdul Karim Bi's absolute authority and strengthened the Kokand Khanate. For the Dzungar Khanate, the massive military and economic losses accelerated the empire's decline and permanently ended its political dominance in Central Asia. Consequently, the Kokand victory directly catalyzed the liberation of the Senior Jüz from Dzungar subjugation.
